subject: anatomy
title: Nasal Cavity: Septum, Kiesselbach Plexus, and Conchal Meatuses

steps.tx: The nasal cavity is divided into right and left halves by a central osteocartilaginous partition designated the nasal septum. The septum is constructed from three principal anatomical components: the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone anterosuperiorly, the **vomer bone** posteroinferiorly, and the quadrilateral septal cartilage anteriorly filling the angular notch between them.
steps.say: The nasal septum divides the nasal cavity. It comprises the perpendicular plate of ethmoid above, the vomer posteroinferiorly, and the quadrilateral septal cartilage anteriorly.

steps.tx: On the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum, approximately one centimetre above and behind the anterior nasal aperture, lies Little area. In this submucosal vascular confluence, four arterial vessels anastomose richly to form the **Kiesselbach plexus**. This vascular network is responsible for over ninety percent of all clinical cases of anterior epistaxis (nosebleeds).
steps.say: In the anteroinferior septum lies Little area, housing the Kiesselbach arterial plexus. Over ninety percent of anterior nosebleeds originate from this vascular confluence.

rows: Enters through anterior ethmoidal foramen down into septum
Traverses sphenopalatine foramen across posterior septum
Ascends incisive canal from hard palate to anterior septum
Sends septal branch across columella into Little area

steps.tx: Kiesselbach plexus is clinically remarkable because it represents an arterial anastomosis between the internal carotid system (via the anterior ethmoidal artery) and the external carotid system (via sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and superior labial arteries). Because the mucosa over Little area is thin and exposed to dry air and digital fingernail trauma, **epistaxis** is exceptionally common in children and dry climates.
steps.say: Kiesselbach plexus links internal and external carotid systems. Thin mucosa and digital trauma make Little area the premier source of anterior childhood epistaxis.

left.title: Anterior Epistaxis (Little Area)
points: Origin: Kiesselbach plexus on anterior septum
Etiology: Digital trauma, dry air, allergic rhinitis
Management: Direct pressure, silver nitrate chemical cautery, packing

right.title: Posterior Epistaxis (Woodruff Plexus)
points: Origin: Sphenopalatine artery branches in lateral wall
Demographic: Elderly patients with severe hypertension
Management: Posterior nasal balloon pack or endoscopic arterial ligation

steps.tx: The lateral wall of the nasal cavity is architecturally complex, expanded by three horizontal scroll-like bony projections designated the conchae (turbinates): superior, middle, and inferior conchae. The superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid bone, whereas the **inferior concha** is an independent skull bone covered by erectile vascular cavernous tissue (swell bodies).
steps.say: Three scroll-like conchae project from the lateral wall: superior, middle, and inferior. The inferior concha is a separate bone covered by erectile cavernous tissue.

rows: Smallest concha; protects olfactory cleft and superior meatus
Overhangs middle meatus; key landmark for functional endoscopic sinus surgery
Largest turbinate; erectile venous sinusoid plexus warms and humidifies air
Triangular recess receiving opening of sphenoidal air sinus

steps.tx: Beneath each turbinate lies a corresponding passage or meatus. The inferior meatus is the largest, lying between the inferior concha and the nasal floor. In its anterior third opens the **nasolacrimal duct**, conveying tears from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity, guarded at its mucosal orifice by the crescentic valve of Hasner, which prevents air entry into the lacrimal system during nose-blowing.
steps.say: Beneath the inferior concha lies the inferior meatus, which receives the nasolacrimal duct. The mucosal valve of Hasner prevents air entry during forceful expiration.

vis.caption: Ostial drainage pathways of the paranasal sinuses and nasolacrimal duct into the nasal meatuses. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The middle meatus is the most clinically critical territory, accommodating the drainage ostia of the majority of paranasal sinuses. Elevating the middle turbinate exposes a rounded mucosal elevation called the bulla ethmoidalis, produced by the middle ethmoidal air cells. Below the bulla curves the **hiatus semilunaris**, a deep crescentic groove terminating anteriorly as the ethmoidal infundibulum.
steps.say: The middle meatus houses the bulla ethmoidalis and hiatus semilunaris. It collects drainage from frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses.

nodes.label: Middle Meatus Exposure (Middle turbinate medialized or resected during FESS)
Bulla Ethmoidalis (Prominence housing middle ethmoidal cells opening on its summit)
Hiatus Semilunaris (Crescentic gutter receiving frontonasal duct anteriorly)
Maxillary Ostium (Opens into floor of posterior half of hiatus semilunaris)

steps.tx: The ostium of the maxillary sinus opens into the floor of the hiatus semilunaris within the middle meatus. Anatomically, the maxillary sinus ostium is situated high up on the medial wall of the antrum, near its roof. This **high ostium** is mechanically disadvantaged because drainage cannot occur by gravity in the erect posture, relying entirely on ciliary mucociliary clearance.
steps.say: The maxillary sinus ostium opens high on its medial wall into the middle meatus. Because it lies near the ceiling, gravity cannot drain the antrum in the standing posture.

left.title: High Maxillary Sinus Ostium
points: Located near the roof of the maxillary antrum
Gravity cannot drain sinus when patient is standing erect
Depends strictly upon active ciliary beat toward ostium
Mucosal edema readily blocks ostium, precipitating acute sinusitis

right.title: Frontal & Ethmoidal Openings
points: Drainage assisted by downward gravitational cascade
Middle ethmoidal cells drain directly on bulla summit
Posterior ethmoidal cells drain into superior meatus

steps.tx: The superior meatus is a narrow slit lying beneath the superior concha, receiving the ostia of the posterior ethmoidal air cells. Above and behind the superior concha lies the triangular sphenoethmoidal recess, which receives the opening of the **sphenoidal sinus**. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) precisely clears these meatal ostia (ostiomeatal complex) to restore physiological mucociliary clearance.
steps.say: The superior meatus drains posterior ethmoid air cells, while the sphenoethmoidal recess drains the sphenoid sinus. Endoscopic surgery clears this ostiomeatal complex.

rows: Above superior concha against sphenoid body
Frontal sinus (via infundibulum), anterior and middle ethmoidal cells, maxillary sinus
